# Answer: Option B

## Issue

The question concerns the statutory basis upon which a party may apply to have a pleading struck out under the *Civil Procedure Act 2011* (NSW) ("CPA").

## Governing Rule

The power to strike out a pleading is conferred by **section 15** of the *Civil Procedure Act 2011* (NSW), which provides:

> **s 15(1):** The court may, on application by a party, strike out a pleading if—
> (a) the pleading does not disclose a reasonable cause of action or defence, or
> (b) the pleading is an abuse of the process of the court, or
> (c) there is no reasonable likelihood that any trial or hearing will take place, or
> (d) the party to whom the pleading is directed is unable to respond to the pleading.

The equivalent provision in the *Civil Procedure Rules 2005* (NSW) Sch 1 is **Rule 14.2**, which mirrors this statutory scheme.

## Application

**Option B is correct.** It accurately captures the grounds in s 15: a pleading may be struck out where it (i) discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence [s 15(1)(a)], (ii) is frivolous, vexatious, or an abuse of the court's process [s 15(1)(b); cf s 15(1)(c)], or (iii) may prejudice a fair trial [s 15(1)(d), where the opposing party is unable to respond].

**Option A is wrong.** Mere disagreement with the other side's legal argument is not a ground for striking out. The court does not resolve substantive disputes at the strike-out stage; it only intervens where the pleading is legally untenable. As the High Court explained in *Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Black Insurance Services (Australia) Pty Ltd* (2009) 239 CLR 205 at [20]–[21], the power is not to be exercised to decide contested questions of fact or law that require evidence or argument.

**Option C is wrong.** A pleading is not struck out merely because it is "factually wrong." Strike-out operates on the *allegations as pleaded*, treating them as admitted; factual disputes are for trial, not for pre-trial disposal. See *Grimshaw v Federal Commissioner of Taxation* (2005) 143 FCR 325.

**Option D is wrong.** Section 15(1) expressly provides for strike-out "on application by a party." The power is therefore available on application, not exclusively at the judge's own initiative.

## Conclusion

A party may apply to strike out a pleading under **s 15(1)** of the *Civil Procedure Act 2011* (NSW) where the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence, is an abuse of process, is unlikely to proceed to trial, or prevents the opposing party from responding. **Option B** correctly states this basis.
